<reason>Side A won by correctly framing the proposition as a sequencing mechanism rather than exclusion, thereby neutralizing Side B's displacement argument. Side A provided a concrete, plausible enforcement mechanism (non-transferable tickets tied to verifiable local identity) that blunted the arbitrage critique, and effectively countered the tourism-revenue argument by highlighting that dynamic pricing funnels surplus to distant platforms rather than municipal coffers, while locals recirculate spending and pay taxes year-round. Side A's pressure questions exposed a live contradiction in Side B's position (arbitrage vs. verification impossibility), and its Rebuttal 2 answers (A1/A2) successfully narrowed the clash by addressing the fiscal and geographic boundary challenges directly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 7), specifically the A1 answer reframing "displacement" as "sequencing" while noting locals' year-round tax contributions, and the A2 answer resolving the geographic boundary problem by proposing metropolitan commuting zones—effectively neutralizing Side B's strongest economic and fairness attacks while maintaining the proposition's core fairness logic.</best_rebuttal>
